description: We are Minh Truong and Minh Hao from HCMUT, Vietnam, with skills in AI, Python, computer vision, and IoT. We aim to use NISAR and optical imagery to explore urban changes and heat in Ho Chi Minh City. We welcome teammates interested in GIS/SAR, web development, visualization, UI/UX, or environmental science. Join us to build and learn together!
summary:
FireCalendar is a web app that turns NASA's two active-fire records, MODIS (about 1 km, 2000–2025) and VIIRS (375 m, from 2012), into one consistent fire calendar from 2000 to 2025, for any country or any area a user draws on the map.
Adding the two sensors together makes fire activity look like it triples in 2012. The real fire didn't change; VIIRS just sees smaller fires. We fix this by putting every observation on the VIIRS scale before counting. A 7-model stacked GPU ensemble converts MODIS brightness and fire radiative power to VIIRS-equivalent values, cutting mid-infrared error by 62.9%. We then count everything on one unit, the "active cell-day": a 5 km² H3 cell with at least one detection on one day.
Users get a monthly burning calendar, each month compared with its usual level, the most similar past seasons, and CSV downloads. Fire managers, early-warning teams, scientists and land managers can finally ask "is this month unusual?" across 26 years without a sensor change distorting the answer.
details:
What it does

FireCalendar turns NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records into an interactive burning activity calendar. Users select a country, draw a rectangular area or enter coordinates, choose dates, explore mapped activity, compare months and years, and download CSV data or chart images. Our archive spans 2000–2025. Because sensors differ in resolution, sensitivity and observing frequency, we harmonize measurements and separately calibrate calendar activity, reducing misleading comparisons across sensor eras.

Benefits and intended impact

Emergency planners and firefighters can investigate recurring critical periods and focus monitoring. Land managers can examine vegetation-burning patterns; scientists can inspect source-labelled records and export results. Familiar calendar views also make satellite history easier for students and the public to understand.

Our intended impact is better-informed preparedness and environmental decision-making. The prototype supplies historical context, not operational emergency alerts. Response-time improvements, avoided fires and emissions benefits remain outcomes to evaluate with users.

How the pipeline works

We standardize UTC times, units and quality information, then assign detection centers to H3 resolution 7, with a mean hexagon area of about 5.16 km². Bounded five-minute platform snapshots feed representative-time windows within 15 minutes. Day/night and hotspot type remain separate. Qualified MIR/TIR medians and snapshot FRP sums form one representative record per sensor family and window.

The physical harmonization model learns MODIS-to-VIIRS-like MIR, TIR and FRP from 57 MODIS-side features. Seven tree and deep tabular learners are blended with validation-based calibration, including empirical quantile mapping where enabled and FRP tail adjustment. Training and internal validation use 2013–2022; evaluation uses 2023–2025 pairs. Observed VIIRS values remain distinguishable from MODIS-derived estimates.

A separate calendar method counts active cell-days and uses S-NPP as the VIIRS reference. Month-specific overlap factors adjust eligible earlier MODIS counts; native S-NPP is used from February 2012. Unsupported early periods remain unavailable in the combined series. This does not reconstruct small fires missed by MODIS.

The documented evaluation on 276,903 pairs reports MIR MAE decreasing from 19.086 to 7.091 K, TIR MAE from 4.543 to 3.393 K, and FRP RMSE from 216.237 to 95.667 MW. These are cross-sensor results, not ground-based validation.

Calendar tools and implementation

A year-by-month heatmap reveals seasonal patterns. Selecting a month opens the daily calendar and updates the map. An active cell-day means one H3 cell with at least one detection on one day; it is not an independent fire incident or a measure of burned area.

Tools and hardware

Python, SQL, DuckDB, Pandas, NumPy, H3 and Parquet support data processing. XGBoost, CatBoost, PyTorch, scikit-learn and SciPy support model development. FastAPI serves precomputed tables to a React and TypeScript application built with Vite and Tailwind CSS. MapLibre and h3-js power maps; Apache ECharts powers plots. Google Colab provides GPU training, while aggregation and similarity analysis run on CPUs. Users need only a browser. Docker packaging supports deployment.

Creativity and design factors

Our contribution connects sensor harmonization, calendar exploration and historical-season matching in one user journey. We treat physical-value calibration and detection-frequency calibration separately. We considered source quality, geometry, repeated overpasses, missing observations, temporal leakage, geographic boundaries and large-data query costs. Precomputed tables keep expensive processing out of interactive requests. Clear units, source labels, shareable selections and downloadable results support interpretation and reuse.

Some regional discontinuities and extreme-fire underestimation remain. The current archive ends in December 2025; adding recent observations and validating cross-region behavior are next steps.

Historical analogs with Cosine and DTW

We reduce repeated observations to H3 cell-days, then build weekly FRP, normalized MIR–TIR contrast and confidence-weighted features. Earlier years are compared over the same completed weeks up to the selected cutoff. Cosine similarity checks week-by-week shape; banded multivariate DTW allows shifts of up to two weeks. Their equally weighted scores rank historical analogs.

This combination makes seasonal comparisons flexible and explainable. A high match describes shape, not the same activity magnitude or a forecast. The analog workflow currently uses a different satellite mix from the calibrated calendar, which requires further validation.

Video Demo

To see FireCalendar in action, please watch the project demonstration video.
